I re-read Pirsig about a year ago, mostly to test whether it still held up (last reading was as an edgy high-schooler during breaks as a dishwasher). I remember the head chef coming in, he'd been a wild man in his youth, and sort of snorting when he saw I was reading it, but kindly of course. I also ride motorcycles with a kind of religiosity. Oh, and I program. So yeah, this hits for me.

I've been working through a lot of the same questions as you, Sinclair, and likewise have been posting as I go through the process. The tension I held in my head was more of a Quality vs poshlost' thing, slightly moreso than Quality vis-a-vis the "craftsman ethos" your post describes. If we are only measuring the output of the machine, and assume it gets "better enough" in time, then yeah it's probably time to take out the sackcloth and ashes if it supplants the self-as-craftsman. I don't think that's quite right, though, or at least it strikes me as premature.

I've got 3 kids so I can relate to the existential anxiety-by-proxy. For myself, I ended up abandoning the argument against AI on qualitative (small-q) terms. My fear is what it means when I stop thinking critically and fire up chat to feed me the answers, and expanding outwards, what this means culturally and how it dictates what gets rewarded (economically). Going to be a wild next 5 years. Thanks for sharing your thoughts, they're valuable.

fwiw, i've used perplexity pretty extensively whenever i'm troubleshooting some linux issue or configuring something. last time when i wanted to set up spotify-qt with librespot, or when i was setting up snapper on fedora with btrfs.

even if i don't fully understand all the commands, i can generally tell if i like the direction it's going, and if i don't like it, i push back, asking for feedback for the solution that i think might work.

perplexity's nice because it's built around web search, so it usually doesen't make stuff up, but nowadays even claude and chatgpt can browse the web, i'm just used to perplexity.

i think that the main advantage for me is that it saves me a lot of frustration. in the past, i would often spend ages browsing through old archived forums, trying solution after solution, which didn't work, and when i finally fixed it, most of what i felt wasn't satisfaction that i solved the problem, but rather that i can finally stop spending time on this. basically i'm not a huge fan of the act of troubleshooting - i would just rather have the system work as i expect it to :)

before perplexity, i had that one linux friend i would annoy about stuff like this, but ever since he started college and got a job, he doesen't have that much time to help me troubleshoot some linux issue for 4 hours in the middle of the night.

The evaluator/prompter can. It's how miscompilations and misoptimizations are found in existing compilers.


Compilers perform a very well defined transformation from input to behavior.


The behavior is defined. The transformation is not.

If you have a set of bitwise and ternary expressions with bit operations, theres hundreds of ways to get that behavior; Could it vpternlog with a vblendmp at the end for multiple instances? Could it cmp+branch for each one? Could it eager-eval then cmov? These decisions and their various heuristics change across compiler versions.

Only a few years ago, you had to use inline asm to get clang to emit lock bts on x86. Now, it understands the semantics of atomic_fetch_or_*, the args going into it, and how its result is operated on, such that you can write the semantically equiv without hacks to get lock bts codegen. But if it can't figure some aspects out, it still falls back to a lock cmpxchg loop. The transformations (or "mental model") is something intuitively built up as you use the specific tool, not defined somewhere. This applies to LLMs as well.

text:
Please do, because truth be told, I'm still not sure which side is right about this, though as my recent posts show, I've lately vacillated back to the side that says we should resist and abstain from using genAI, to try to put the brakes on this problematic new thing.

On the one hand, as we all know, there are people who are absolutely convinced that the ethical problems outweigh all benefits, and that by focusing on the benefits that we gain while ignoring the costs that are mostly born by others, we're being selfish. This rant by Larry Garfield crossed my Mastodon timeline the other day, and it hit me hard. He's absolutely certain that the ethical problems outweigh the benefits, and this has now put him in the hard position of having to choose between grudgingly, angrily using genAI in his next job, and not working in software development at all. And -- this is the kicker -- he blames all of us who have not fought the normalization of genAI usage, for making it inevitable.

On the other hand, I have to reckon with the fact that the rise of genAI, including coding agents, is having a positive impact in a community that I care about and am part of, namely, the blind community. There's a new wave of software being developed by and for blind people, just within the past few months, and at least some of it, maybe most of it, is being written with the help of coding agents. Of course, a possible retort to that is that the benefits to us blind people who are using PCs in the first place, and could thus be considered relatively privileged, don't offset the costs that are born by less privileged people elsewhere that we tend not to be aware of.

So in the end, the strongest evidence I have that the negative side outweighs the positive is the absolute conviction of the people who take that position, at least one of whom (the author of the post I linked above) now finds himself in what he perceives to be a real moral quandary as a result. But of course, those people could be misguided. I grew up immersed in evangelical Christianity, surrounded by people who were absolutely certain that it was the one true way. I no longer believe that, because I now think the factual claims are wrong, and no amount of certainty and passion can make up for that. But in this case, I'm not yet convinced that the factual claims about the ethical problems with genAI are wrong. You've even acknowledged that at least one of the problems -- the fact that the model developers use copyrighted work without consent -- can't be refuted. And you've recently said that there's a good indirect reason to believe that the electricity and water usage of genAI models is bad -- the fact that the companies aren't disclosing actual numbers. So, unlike with my rejection of religion, I can't yet be sure that I'm off the hook.

text:
My house runs on 100% renewable energy (thanks to Idaho Powers green energy option)


As a tangent, this is Complicated. Some facts about the energy grid:


Your house is connected to the same grid, and receiving the same electrons, as all of your neighbors. There's no way to route specific electrons to you.



And this grid is probably connected in some way or another to a continent-wide electrical system, though it gets complicated as transmission capacity between regions is often limited.



Generally speaking, renewable energy sources provide output independent of demand - you can't turn up the wind because you need more capacity. On the other hand, fossil fuel generation is a lot more flexible - you put in as much fuel as you need for the demand, and get that much energy out. (Obviously there is an upper limit, but in a functioning system you don't hit that limit.)


Because of point 1, "100% green energy" is entirely an accounting notion - in practice there's just a bunch of generation plugged into a bunch of houses and it's entirely irrelevant which electrons go where, but notionally each kilowatt-hour you use corresponds to a kilowatt-hour that was generated renewably.

But you live in an area where a nontrivial percentage of electricity generation is fossil fuels. You turn on your stove, increasing demand. What happens? They can't turn up the wind or the sun, so they start burning more fossil fuels. From an accounting perspective, you were on 100% green energy before, and you still are - but then someone else, who wasn't on 100% green energy but was "getting" some green energy anyway, is now getting a larger share of fossil-fuel energy. You ultimately can't escape the fact that by using more electricity, you're creating more demand, and that demand is being met - at least in part - with fossil fuels.

(None of this is my area of expertise! And I'm definitely papering over a lot of complexity. So very happy to be corrected.)

This may be one of the most resonant posts I've seen on this subject and my own reaction to it. I find myself curious how similar the author and I are in age/experience. Especially this paragraph in particular:


Part of that is taste and part of it is control. I attempt to set a high bar for what I want code to look like, and I want to understand the code I ship. Under pressure, or in a discussion with another human, I want to be able to explain what the system does without first having to ask a clanker to explain it to me. Now there is obviously a question if this desire to understand the code is one that I will still have a few years from now. For now I have not moved past the point of comprehension being important to me.


A few days ago, when Fable was available, I decided to have it write a chunk of C code for me. We do updates of firmware over BLE. And I wanted to entertain a wire protocol variant. The device has a wire protocol already, so it's really just abstracting out the upgrade engine so it could be driven by either BLE or the wire engine, and then adding the commands/events to the wire protocol. Fable did a decent job. I had to steer it a couple of times and, as the author points out, tell it not to stress about certain conditions that I know from external context are just not possible. It was about 2.5 hours of bot-sitting. About $40 of tokens. It was kind of boring. I prompted, played BZFlag until I heard the "done" beep, checked in, adjusted, then shot more tanks. My big misgiving at the end was that I did not "know" the code. Not that I remember every bit of code I've ever written, but often when visiting old code, it's like reacquainting with an old friend. And in this case, that just wasn't the case. I could do some test runs, and I'm reasonably sure it would work. But there is a discovery process when writing code, where as you're expressing the algorithm, your brain sees "ah, there's an edge/corner case here, I need to wrestle with whether to worry about that and if it is a concern, how to mitigate". Without doing the journey myself, I could not feel comfortable that the decently written code was really what I wanted in all cases, not just the happy paths.

So I wrote the code myself. Took 2 hours tops with Zed's very useful autocomplete. I was happier with the code I wrote. I knew it. And then I asked Claude to take a look at it. It sycophantically commended my work and pointed out "used the wrong variable here" (which both had the same type, so yay for type safety, eh?). I was much happier with this model. It cost the company less.

Put yourself in my position for a moment. I spent a couple of hours writing that article after several days of fairly extensive experimentation. It then led to a number of thoughtful responses from people who actually read it, including on Bluesky, Twitter, and Hacker News.

Then I see the post submitted here, click into the comments, and the first thing I find is a snarky, dismissive accusation that it is self-promo spam, speculation, and doomtrolling.

Maybe I have too high an expectation for the quality of discussion here, but I don’t think replies like that add much. If you don't find the piece worth reading or thinking about, that's completely fine. But accusing someone of spam and bad faith without engaging with what they wrote does not make the conversation better.


Sure smells like doomtrolling to me


Well then have that opinion, but if you read the post you will probably have found that there is quite a bit of nuance to this. Nothing in this post says that the world will end, far from it. Neither do I believe it, nor did I write it.
